newsitem.title: USA: Florida town wants to apologize to Robinson.
newsitem.headline: Florida town wants to apologize to Robinson.

text.p: A Florida town that kicked Jackie Robinson off its baseball field 51 years ago said Wednesday it wants to apologise to Robinson's family for what one city leader called "a stain ... on our soul."

Police in Sanford, a city of about 35,000 just north of Orlando, escorted Robinson off the field at Municipal Park when he visited in February 1946 for an exhibition game between the minor league Montreal Royals and their parent club, the Brooklyn Dodgers.
The game took place during spring training a year before Robinson, then with the Royals, made his debut with the Dodgers and broke major league baseball's colour barrier.

"The city of Sanford, much like most small towns in the South those days, had an ordinance that prohibited blacks and whites playing together on city-owned land," Sanford Mayor Larry Dale said. "Back in 1946, it was a different era down here."

Police Chief Roy Williams was called to the stadium by a fan angry at Robinson's presence. After Robinson was walked to the dugout, Williams announced that Sanford would let him play only three innings per game at the park.
Robinson also was allowed to perform windsprints and drills with teammates at the park, although he had to stay with a black family rather than at the team's hotel.
"I guess it was a compromise. Chief Williams was known sort of as a negotiator," Dale said.
Other towns across Florida, long a home to baseball's pre-season spring training camps, cancelled games rather than allow Robinson to play.

Dale said city leaders had decided to apologise to Robinson's family and the Dodgers, now in Los Angeles, during a commission meeting Monday night. He said the town intended to send a letter and issue a proclamation, but had not yet been able to convey the formal apology.

Baseball marked the 50th anniversary of Robinson's Major League debut in a celebration at New York's Shea Stadium Tuesday night. The game was interrupted in the fifth inning for a tribute led by President Clinton.
